title: The North & Final Round
subtitle: The three territories, then a mixed finale across the whole guide

questions.question: What does "Nunavut" mean in Inuktitut?
questions.explanation: Nunavut means "our land" in Inuktitut. It was established in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories. The population is about 85% Inuit and Inuktitut is an official language.

questions.question: What is the capital of Nunavut, and what was it formerly called?
questions.explanation: The capital of Nunavut is Iqaluit, formerly Frobisher Bay, named after the English explorer Martin Frobisher, who penetrated the uncharted Arctic for Queen Elizabeth I in 1576.

questions.question: How does Nunavut's 19-member Legislative Assembly choose its premier and ministers?
questions.explanation: The 19-member Legislative Assembly of Nunavut chooses a premier and ministers by consensus rather than through political parties.

questions.question: Which territorial capital is called the "diamond capital of North America"?
questions.explanation: Yellowknife (population 20,000), capital of the Northwest Territories, is called the diamond capital of North America. More than half the N.W.T. population is Aboriginal (Dene, Inuit and Métis).

questions.question: At 4,200 kilometres, which is the second-longest river system in North America?
questions.explanation: The Mackenzie River, at 4,200 kilometres, is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi and drains an area of 1.8 million square kilometres.

questions.question: Why is the North often referred to as the "Land of the Midnight Sun"?
options: Because the sun is red at night
Because at the height of summer daylight can last up to 24 hours
Because the sun never rises in summer
questions.explanation: At the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours. In winter the sun disappears and darkness sets in for three months. The territories hold one-third of Canada's land mass but only about 100,000 people.

questions.question: Thousands of miners came to the Yukon during the Gold Rush of which decade, celebrated in the poetry of Robert W. Service?
questions.explanation: Thousands of miners came to the Yukon during the Gold Rush of the 1890s, as celebrated in the poetry of Robert W. Service. The White Pass and Yukon Railway opened from Skagway, Alaska, to Whitehorse in 1900.

questions.question: Where is Mount Logan, the highest mountain in Canada?
questions.explanation: Mount Logan, in the Yukon, is the highest mountain in Canada. It is named for Sir William Logan, who founded the Geological Survey of Canada. Yukon also holds the record for Canada's coldest temperature (-63°C).

questions.question: Who are the Canadian Rangers?
options: Part of the Canadian Forces Reserves who patrol the Arctic drawing on indigenous knowledge
questions.explanation: The Canadian Rangers, part of the Canadian Forces Reserves (militia), draw on indigenous knowledge and travel by snowmobile and all-terrain vehicle from Resolute to the Magnetic North Pole, keeping the flag flying in Canada's Arctic.

questions.question: What is the capital of Yukon?
questions.explanation: Whitehorse is the capital of Yukon. Yellowknife is the capital of the Northwest Territories, and Iqaluit of Nunavut.

questions.question: Identify four rights that Canadians enjoy.
options: Free housing, free cars, free food, free travel
Mobility rights, Aboriginal peoples' rights, official language and minority language educational rights, and multiculturalism
The right to bear arms, to secede, to refuse jury duty and to avoid taxes
The right to vote at 16, to a pension at 50, to free university and to a passport
questions.explanation: The Charter sets out rights including Mobility Rights, Aboriginal Peoples' Rights, Official Language Rights and Minority Language Educational Rights, and Multiculturalism. The right to vote and the right to apply for a passport are also commonly cited.

questions.question: Name two Canadian symbols.
options: The maple leaf and the beaver
questions.explanation: Important Canadian symbols include the Crown, the flag, the maple leaf, the fleur-de-lys, the coat of arms, the Parliament Buildings, the beaver, the RCMP, hockey and the Victoria Cross.

questions.question: In the territories, which official represents the federal government, and in the provinces which official represents the Sovereign?
questions.explanation: In the three territories the Commissioner represents the federal government and plays a ceremonial role. In each province the Lieutenant Governor represents the Sovereign.

questions.question: Put these events in the correct order: (1) Confederation, (2) Battle of the Plains of Abraham, (3) War of 1812, (4) Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
questions.explanation: Plains of Abraham (1759), War of 1812, Confederation (1867), Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982).
questions.ref: Discover Canada, Canada's History (p. 14-19) and Rights (p. 8)

questions.question: Which of these events happened in 1982?
options: The Constitution was amended to entrench the Charter and July 1 became Canada Day
questions.explanation: In 1982 the Constitution was amended (without Quebec's agreement) to entrench the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and Dominion Day became Canada Day. The referendum was 1980, the flag 1965, and Nunavut 1999.
questions.ref: Discover Canada, Rights (p. 8), Confederation (p. 18), Canada and Quebec (p. 24)

questions.question: True or false: Because of the cold Arctic climate, there are no trees on the tundra and the soil is permanently frozen.
questions.explanation: True. Much of the North is tundra, the vast rocky Arctic plain. Because of the cold climate there are no trees on the tundra and the soil is permanently frozen (permafrost).

questions.question: True or false: The Northwest Territories were originally made up in 1870 from Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory.
questions.explanation: True. The N.W.T. were originally made up in 1870 from Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory, lands previously controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company.

questions.question: True or false: The Confederation Bridge joins New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island and is the longest bridge in the world over water that freezes in winter.
questions.explanation: True. The Confederation Bridge, almost 13 kilometres long, joins New Brunswick and P.E.I. and is the longest bridge in the world to cross water that freezes in winter.
questions.ref: Discover Canada, Prince Edward Island (p. 46) and photo caption (p. 56)

questions.question: True or false: Nunavut became a territory in 1999, while Newfoundland and Labrador joined Canada in 1949.
questions.explanation: True. Newfoundland and Labrador joined in 1949 as the last province; Nunavut was established in 1999 as the newest territory.
questions.ref: Discover Canada, Expansion of the Dominion (p. 19)

questions.question: True or false: The three territories contain one-third of Canada's land mass but have a population of only about 100,000.
questions.explanation: True. The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Yukon contain one-third of Canada's land mass but have a population of only about 100,000. There are gold, lead, copper, diamond and zinc mines.
